definition: Used so often that it has become stale, dull and unoriginal.
example: The graduation speaker closed with a hackneyed line about following your dreams.
nuance: Hackneyed blames overuse for the dullness; banal can describe something ordinary from the start, even if it was never repeated.
prompt: A writing teacher marks up a student's short story.
options: The teacher circled the hackneyed opening about a dark and stormy night.
The teacher praised the hackneyed plot because no story had ever tried it before.
The hackneyed sentence was so tangled that the teacher read it three times.
A virus had hackneyed the student's laptop, erasing the story's last page.
reasons: That opening has been copied so many times that it now feels worn out.
A plot nobody has tried is new, the opposite of one made stale by repetition.
A confusing sentence is convoluted; the word describes staleness, not difficulty.
This mixes it up with hacked; it is an adjective about tired ideas, not a computer break-in.

practice.prompt: A film critic reviews a new action movie.
options: Hoping to flatter the director, the critic called the dialogue hackneyed.
The critic felt hackneyed after racing across town to catch the late screening.
The critic called the special effects hackneyed since they were the first of their kind.
The critic groaned at the hackneyed twist she had seen in dozens of films.
reasons: The word is a criticism, so using it could never flatter anyone.
Being rushed and worn down is harried; the word describes overused ideas, not people.
Being the first of its kind makes something groundbreaking, not tired from overuse.
A twist repeated across many movies has lost its power to surprise.
